reading.rtitle: Invent Match -- Accounts Payable Automation for SAP
paras: Stop typing invoices. Invent Match is a cloud-based tool that reads every supplier invoice, compares it with the purchase order and the delivery, and sends it to SAP for payment. Most mid-sized finance teams cut invoice processing time by more than half in the first three months.

Out-of-the-box SAP connection. Our pre-built connector links Invent Match to SAP and Oracle in days, not months. There is no new ERP to learn: your team keeps working in the system it already knows, and the integration is seamless.

An intuitive dashboard for the whole team. One screen shows every invoice that is waiting, every exception and every payment due this week. New users learn it in an afternoon, so adoption does not depend on a long training program.
Customizable approval rules. Each company approves invoices in a different way. You choose who signs off which amounts, and Invent Match follows your rules, not ours.

Reliable and robust. Invent Match processes more than two million invoices a year for customers in Brazil and Europe, with 99.9 per cent availability. If the bank changes a file format, our team updates the connector, so your close does not stop.
reading.source: Alumni by Better -- product page written for this lesson, in the format software vendors use on their websites

items.situation: Feature: 'pre-built SAP connector'. Turn it into a benefit with so that.
tips: It has a pre-built SAP connector, so that you go live in days, not months.
Feature + so that + what the customer gains.

items.situation: Put these in the right order: dashboard / new / simple.
tips: Opinion before age: simple, then new.

items.situation: Put these in the right order: tool / cloud-based / small.
tips: Size before type: small, then cloud-based.

items.situation: Marta asks: what does 'out-of-the-box' mean for my customers? Answer in plain English.
tips: It means they can use the SAP connection immediately, with no extra development.
Explain the adjective with what the customer does.

items.situation: Say the collocation: the integration is ___ (smooth, no breaks).
tips: The integration is seamless. A seamless integration.
Seamless goes with integration, experience, transition.

items.situation: Marta says every vendor calls itself 'innovative'. Answer with a number instead.
tips: Fair point. We process more than two million invoices a year, with 99.9 per cent availability.
A number is more convincing than an empty adjective.

listenings.text: I write product pages for software companies, and I have one test for every sentence. I call it the so what test. Our tool has a pre-built SAP connector. So what? So you go live in days, not months. The first sentence is a feature. The second is a benefit, and the benefit is the one the customer remembers. Most engineers write pages full of features, because they built them and they are proud of them. A buyer does not care what the tool has. A buyer cares about what changes on Monday morning. The other thing I fix is adjectives. People write things like an innovative powerful new smart solution. Four adjectives, zero information. One good adjective in the right place is better than four, and a number is better than any adjective.

Before a first call with a vendor, I spend about two minutes on their product page. I skip every word that every vendor uses: innovative, world-class, next-generation. Those words tell me nothing. What I look for is three things. First, does it connect to the system we already have, and how long does that take? Second, who on my team will use it, and do they need training? And third, is there a number I can check, like how many customers or how many invoices a year? When a page answers those three questions in the first screen, I go to the call with good questions. When it does not, I go to the call with doubts, and the salesperson has to work much harder.
